analysis.one_liner: Spends about $1.7 trillion over ten years to retrofit public schools, hire staff, and fund disability education.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2026 with 17 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was sent to two House committees and has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would pour federal money into public schools on a scale far beyond current spending: grants to convert school buildings to zero-carbon, all-electric facilities with clean air and water; block grants to hire teachers, counselors, nurses, and other staff for ten years in high-need districts; climate-resiliency projects like solar power, electric buses, and backup energy; a fully funded federal share of special education rising to 40 percent over a decade; and a large increase in Title I money for low-income schools. It comes with wage rules (construction workers must be paid local prevailing wages), Buy American requirements, and local-hiring goals. The money is mandatory — it would be spent automatically over ten years without a new vote each year — and the bill does not name a tax or offset to pay for it.
analysis.who_benefits: Students in under-resourced schools get repaired, healthier buildings and more counselors, nurses, and teachers. School support staff and paraprofessionals get raises and training pathways. Construction and clean-energy workers get a decade of jobs at prevailing wages with apprenticeship slots. Districts serving children with disabilities get the federal special-education share raised toward the 40 percent promised in 1975 but never delivered.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students, school staff, and construction workers

how_it_helps.text: Provides grants covering 100 percent of the cost of converting the one-third most vulnerable (highest-need) schools to 'healthy zero-carbon schools' with clean air, no asbestos or lead, all-electric heating, and onsite renewable energy [S2].

Provides $250 billion in block grants over ten years for high-need districts to hire teachers, counselors, psychologists, nurses, librarians, and paraprofessionals for ten years, and to raise paraprofessional pay [S2].

Mandatorily funds the federal share of special education (IDEA), rising from about $6.4 billion to $69.6 billion a year and reaching the 40-percent funding level by 2036, and adds $74 billion a year for Title I low-income school funding [S2].

Requires Davis-Bacon prevailing wages, registered apprenticeship use, project labor agreements on large projects, and local hiring for school construction jobs, and bars contractors from using staffing-agency labor except in acute shortages [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The bill funds everything through mandatory appropriations from the Treasury without naming any tax, fee, or spending offset, so the roughly $1.7 trillion ten-year cost would be deficit-financed unless Congress separately raises revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and the national debt

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates about $1.7 trillion over ten years with no identified revenue source, adding directly to federal deficits and debt [S2].

The labor and procurement rules are prescriptive: prevailing-wage requirements, project labor agreements on projects of $25 million or more, union-neutrality policies, and apprenticeship quotas can raise construction costs and shrink the pool of eligible contractors, which can slow projects and reduce how far each dollar goes [S2].

The retrofit standard is a single federal definition of a 'healthy zero-carbon school' — all-electric systems, specified energy-performance numbers, and new buildings at least 2,500 feet from any oil or gas well — leaving districts little flexibility to adapt designs to local conditions and costs [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and large: many school buildings are old, hot, moldy, or energy-inefficient, the federal special-education share is decades below its promise, and poor districts cannot hire enough counselors and nurses. But the design carries serious costs an honest supporter must acknowledge: the entire price is deficit-financed with no funding mechanism in the bill, the one-size-fits-all building standard and dense labor mandates will likely make retrofits more expensive per school than a more flexible program would, and $740 billion in new Title I money on top of existing appropriations represents a sweeping federal takeover of what has been a shared funding responsibility.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late July 2026 and referred to the Education and Workforce and Energy and Commerce committees, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on July 27, 2026 [S1][S2].
Seventeen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican or Independent cosponsor appears on the list [S3].
The bill was referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce and the Committee on Energy and Commerce [S4].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the action history after the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost anything: the bill has not moved, so school buildings and staffing stay as they are, and no federal money has been committed or saved. If it dies without a vote, the beneficiaries of inaction will be the status quo — districts that rely on local property wealth, and contractors who prefer building to the old standard.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo holds; nothing gained, nothing lost

sides.party_line_note: All 18 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats, none is a Republican, and the bill sits in committees controlled by the 223-seat House Republican majority with no recorded movement.

industries.industry: School construction, HVAC, and electrical contractors
industries.note: A decade of $446 billion in retrofit and construction grants would be a historic contract pipeline for these firms, at prevailing wages with apprenticeship requirements. Students get the healthier buildings the same money produces, so the industry's gain and the public's gain run together here — though the labor mandates favor unionized and larger contractors over small non-union shops.

industries.industry: Solar, battery, and clean-energy equipment makers
industries.note: The bill pushes schools to install onsite solar and storage, buy electric school buses, and electrify kitchens and heating, and requires American-made products, creating a large guaranteed demand for these industries. Cleaner air and lower energy bills for schools come alongside the manufacturers' sales.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel industry (heating oil, natural gas, propane suppliers to schools)
industries.note: The bill requires all-electric heating, water heating, lighting, and cooking in retrofitted and new schools, and bars new school construction within 2,500 feet of an oil or gas well. It would progressively remove schools from these companies' customer base.

The bill bars contractors from hiring through temp agencies on funded projects except in certified acute short-term shortages, cutting into a labor middleman business. Workers gain direct employment and prevailing wages instead.

The bill makes all new federally funded school positions part of existing bargaining units and requires union-neutrality policies where none exists, locking the unionized model into the expanded school workforce. The positions themselves also directly serve students, so the entrenchment comes bundled with real public benefit.

analysis.trajectory: With about five months left in this Congress, a Republican House majority, no committee action since the July referral, and no Republican cosponsors, the realistic path is that the bill dies at the end of this Congress without a hearing or vote. Its backers' usual route at this stage is reintroduction in the next Congress.
